transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-28 3:00pm PT | Duration: ~52 minutes | Attendees: Ari Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Leo Grant (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (CTO, Stellarnet), Priya Singh (Head of Infrastructure), Diego Alvarez (Security), Marta Lopez (Platform)

[00:00] Ari: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — Ari Chen from Redwood, Maya Patel our SE, Leo on solutions. Tom/Priya/Diego, thanks for making time. we wanted to use this to scope the POC around private networking and data residency — make sure we align on success criteria and benchmarks.

[00:18] Tom: yeah thanks. we built some internal LLM features but performance/cost tradeoffs are killing us. main blockers: we need the inference to run inside our VPC or via PrivateLink, EU data residency for a subset of traffic, and tight egress controls. we want a pilot to validate latency and throughput and to see cost delta for different configs.

[00:39] Maya: great. first question — what does success look like for you? latency p90/p95 targets, throughput, cost targets, or functional correctness?

[00:50] Priya: operationally: p95 under 200ms for typical chat completions (we're usually 256 tokens, occasionally 512). we have peaks at about 150 concurrent users doing interactive flows — ballpark peak concurrency maybe 200 sessions, steady around 40-60. throughput target for POC about 150-250 requests per second to validate autoscaling. also need to understand token-based cost at that load.

[01:15] Diego: from security: data must not leave the EU for EU customers. encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration, and we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. also need the option to restrict egress to our NAT gateway and have IP allowlisting.

[01:32] Ari: okay that's helpful. so we'll propose a scoped POC: 2 weeks to set up networking + private endpoints, 1 week baseline functional test, 1 week of benchmark runs, then 1-2 weeks to iterate — roughly 4-6 weeks total. during setup we'll help set up either VPC peering or AWS PrivateLink depending on your preference and constraints.

[01:52] Priya: can you outline the differences operationally? we're on AWS (eu-central-1) for our EU data, but we also have services in us-west-2 for non-EU traffic.

[02:04] Leo: sure — brief tradeoffs: VPC peering gives you direct routing between your VPC and the Redwood VPC — it's straightforward but requires route table updates and potential cross-account peering. PrivateLink (AWS NLB endpoints) exposes an interface endpoint in your VPC and avoids some route table changes, typically simpler for private connectivity and better for controlled egress via your NAT. PrivateLink also makes it easier for you to restrict traffic to explicit endpoints. Performance-wise both can achieve production latencies; PrivateLink might add a tiny additional hop but is often negligible. for our Dedicated/Private offering we support both.

[02:40] Tom: what about cross-region? EU traffic must stay in eu-central-1. Non-EU can use hosted or dedicated in other regions. how do you ensure data residency separation?

[02:53] Maya: we can pin workloads to specific regions — for EU traffic we'll provision inference capacity and a private endpoint in eu-central-1. logs and model artifacts for that environment can also be kept in that region. we'll propose a network diagram showing isolated routing and a separate account for EU tenancy per your compliance needs.

[03:10] Priya: egress — our security team wants all outbound traffic to go through our NAT and be monitored. can Redwood's endpoints be routed that way?

[03:19] Ari: yes, with PrivateLink or peering you can control the path. we'll include recommended NAT gateway and route table configs in the diagram. You can also configure IP-level allowlist on our side for inbound connections from your VPC ranges.

[03:34] Diego: how does authentication look? SAML/SSO for console is fine; but for API we need cert-based or mTLS?

[03:42] Maya: for the POC we'll use short-lived API keys scoped to the pilot environment and mutual TLS is supported on our PrivateLink endpoints. for production we can integrate with your KMS for key wrapping and with your identity provider for provisioning. we'll note that in the security pack.

[03:59] Tom: benchmarks — what tests do you recommend?

[04:05] Maya: typical plan: we run a set of latency tests (single-request p50/p95/p99) with varied token lengths (128, 256, 512). throughput tests with increasing concurrency to determine sustained rps and tail latency under load. include batching scenarios to measure cost/throughput trade-offs. we'll instrument with detailed token-level latency and GPU utilization traces.

[04:30] Leo: concrete benchmarking parameters we propose: 1) baseline single-client p95 using 256 tokens, 2) sustained throughput test at your target concurrency (start at 50, 100, 200 concurrent sessions), 3) peak burst test for autoscale check, 4) memory/KV cache behavior for multi-turn chat. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU/util, and cost estimates.

[04:55] Priya: sample payloads — our average messages are ~40 tokens, responses average 200-350 tokens. can we share a sanitized sample dataset?

[05:05] Tom: yes we'll sanitize and send.

[05:09] Maya: great. a couple of clarifications on success criteria: you mentioned p95 <200ms for interactive flows — is that for full 256 token generation end-to-end or per-chunk streaming latency?

[05:21] Priya: full completion. that's the business requirement for a fast chat UI. if that's unrealistic we'll accept streaming with per-chunk p95 <100ms but would prefer full completion under 200ms.

[05:33] Ari: noting that, we'll include two acceptance thresholds: 1) full completion p95 <200ms for 256 token sequences under target concurrency OR 2) streaming per-chunk p95 <100ms with steady user-perceived latency under 300ms. We'll make both part of the POC evaluation.

[05:50] Diego: logging and audit — we need request/response hashes logged and stored in our EU account. are you able to forward audit logs to our SIEM via Kinesis or syslog?

[06:03] Leo: we support log forwarding and can push structured audit logs to your ingestion endpoint (Kinesis, S3, or syslog over TLS). for EU-resident traffic we can ensure logs stay in the region. we'll include retention policy options in the security doc.

[06:20] Tom: cost sensitivity — curious about unit cost vs hosted public endpoints. want ballpark delta for private networking and dedicated pools.

[06:29] Ari: expectation: dedicated/private with VPC peering or PrivateLink will be higher than public hosted by a margin depending on committed capacity. we'll give estimates in the pricing sheet — for the POC we can run on small dedicated pool sizes to measure real token costs and extrapolate.

[06:45] Priya: what about model variants / quantization? we'd like to test both a full-precision and a quantized variant to measure latency vs quality.

[06:54] Maya: yes — we'll include a quantized variant test. POC plan: run the same prompts against full FP model and quantized 4-bit/8-bit variant, capture latency, perplexity/quality metrics (if you have eval prompts) and token costs.

[07:10] Marta: timeline again? you said 4-6 weeks. can you break that into concrete milestones we can put into our calendar?

[07:18] Ari: sure. Milestone 0: finalize scope and network agreement (this week) — we send network diagram and security pack. Milestone 1 (week 1-2): network setup and endpoint provisioning, private endpoints in eu-central-1. Milestone 2 (week 3): baseline functional testing and integration. Milestone 3 (week 4): benchmark runs and data collection. Milestone 4 (week 5-6): analysis, follow-ups, and decision gate. we'll propose exact dates once we get your preferred windows.

[07:50] Tom: how much lift on our side? we have a small infra team.

[07:54] Ari: typically we need: IAM role or peering approvals, some route table changes, a temporary API key, and access to a test SIEM endpoint for log forwarding. Maya will provide the exact network requirements doc to reduce back-and-forth.

[08:08] Diego: for compliance, can you run an on-prem package? we'd prefer a private control plane but currently want to try PrivateLink into your hosted private capacity first.

[08:18] Leo: we have both Private (VPC/on-prem) and Dedicated offerings. for the POC we'll recommend PrivateLink into our EU-dedicated cluster which keeps traffic in-region and still gives you managed infra; if you need later we can explore an on-prem appliance.

[08:33] Priya: one more thing — NAT egress costs and firewall rules. we'll need to confirm data exfil prevention policies.

[08:41] Maya: we'll include recommended egress patterns and notes on how to ensure no unintended external egress. plus details on IP ranges and TLS enforcement.

[08:52] Tom: ok sounds good. can you capture the exact acceptance criteria in the POC doc? we want an explicit pass/fail matrix.

[08:58] Ari: yes — we'll produce a POC success criteria table covering performance (p95/p99 thresholds), throughput, quality checks, region residency, security controls, and operational handoff requirements.

[09:10] Priya: anything else on benchmarks? latency under encryption, and with KV cache warm/cold behavior — that matters for chat.

[09:19] Maya: good call — we'll include cold/warm cache tests (first-token vs subsequent tokens) and measure KV cache hit rates. also will include GPU utilization plots.

[09:30] Ari: recap of next steps: Ari will send the network diagram and security pack; Maya will send benchmark plan and test scripts; Priya/Tom will send sanitized sample payloads and traffic profile; Diego will confirm audit/logging retention. propose we meet again after you've reviewed the docs to schedule benchmark windows.

[09:46] Tom: agreed. thanks everyone.

[09:49] Ari: thanks, we'll follow up by end of day tomorrow with docs and timelines.

[09:53] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional filler words, short crosstalk, transcription may have minor name misspellings. References shared: "network-diagram-draft.pdf (link)", "stellarnet-security-questionnaire.xlsx (link)", "benchmark-plan.md (link)".
